newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Europe--background whisper in UK election.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Europe--background whisper in UK election.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major's clash with "Eurosceptics" in his Conservative Party has dominated headlines but few analysts expect the Europe debate to sway many voters in Britain's election.
Four out of 10 Britons say they want Britain to leave the European Union. Across Europe, leaders nervously await the result of what they term a crucial election for the EU's future.
Despite this evidence, politicians and opinion pollsters seriously doubt the issue of Europe will dominate campaigning or crucially influence how more than a few thousand Britons vote.

"Europe is beginning to rise on the agenda, but it's not in the same league as the "Four Horsemen' of public concern -- the health service, education, law and order and unemployment," said Bob Worcester, chairman of the MORI polling organisation.

Anyone listening to British political debate during 1996 would have thought Europe was almost the only issue that mattered. There is no doubt Britons are increasingly uneasy about the whole European Union experiment.
"Eurosceptic" warnings about creeping federalism in the 15-member bloc and the dangers of a single currency have hit home.
An opinion poll last week showed 38 percent of Britons wanted to leave the European Union. This was just four percentage points less than the total of those who wanted to stay in.
In June 1995 when Major, fed up with attacks from Eurosceptic rebels, announced a leadership election, the pro-Europeans led by 32 points.
A separate MORI poll showed in December that Europe ranked second behind the National Health Service when voters were asked about the most important issue in Britain.
But with an election due by May, media attention is already switching from the European issue to more fundamental subjects and, as it does, so public concern will slip away.

"You find that the issues that matter like education are at the foremost of voters' minds and rightly so. I don't think the one big agenda on the minds of the British people is what (Eurosceptic member of parliament) Teresa Gorman says," said Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine this week.

Major has promised that he will target Europe, the economy and the constitution as areas of Labour weakness during the run-up to the election in an attempt to overturn Labour's 20-point lead in opinion polls.
Major believes he can milk the growing anti-European mood in Britain by attacking what he calls Labour's support for increased federalism within the EU.
But, apart from Labour's support for the Social Chapter on workers' rights, most Britons would be hard-pushed to see any difference in the two parties' attitude towards Europe.

Both have promised a referendum on a single currency before Britain joins. Major's steady drift towards an anti-European stance, fuelled by public mistrust of Brussels' influence, has been mirrored by Tony Blair and his party.

"Europe just isn't that important an issue in determining how people vote because there is not a vast difference between the two parties -- there are more internal party differences than external," said Nick Moon of NOP pollsters. "Also, most people don't really understand what it's all about."
A survey by Gallup in December showed Europe ranked fourth among voters asked about the most urgent problem facing Britain -- but it only polled eight percent of the votes.
"It is not a bread-and-butter issue, it's only in the public's mind when the media remind them of it," said Gallup's Bob Wybrow.

The only element of the European debate that could affect the election -- and partly explains Major's decision to target the issue -- is the appearance of the Referendum Party backed by millions of pounds from Sir James Goldsmith.
Goldsmith wants a referendum, now, on Britain's future role in the European Union and has attracted support from disaffected Conservative voters. The party claims more than 100,000 members.
Pollsters say there is no chance Goldsmith's party could win a seat, as it is polling a maximum of three percent.
But he could embarrass Major by seducing enough voters in marginal seats, particularly where the Conservative candidates are pro-European, to allow one of the opposition parties to win.
"The Conservatives could lose that seat and possibly the election if the Referendum Party muddies the water enough," said Wybrow.
